items.prose: The interviewer: "Make me a market on the sum of four dice, width at most 2." Work at interview pace: about a minute.
items.question: What is your bid?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the fair value of four dice, then step down half the width.

byKey.width: You stepped down the whole width. Each side sits half the width from 14.
byKey.fair: That is the fair value. Your bid sits below it.

explain.text: Four dice average $4 \times 3.5 = 14$. Width 2 puts the bid at 13 and the ask at 15. Say it as "13 at 15".

items.prose: You pay £2.50 to roll two dice and are paid the smaller face in pounds. The smaller of two dice averages 91/36.
items.question: What is your edge per play, in pounds? Give four decimal places.

byKey.sign: You took the payout from the stake. 91/36 is just above 2.50.
byKey.larger: You used the larger face, 161/36. The game pays the smaller.

explain.text: The game is worth $91/36 \approx 2.5278$ and costs 2.50. The edge is $1/36$, under 3p a play. It is positive but tiny, so the variance swamps it over a few plays.

items.prose: Three dice, fair value 10.5, half-width 1. This interviewer's rule skews 0.5 a unit. They sell you 2.
items.question: What is your new ask?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Long 2 means $q = +2$ in $m = V - \gamma q$.

byKey.sign: You moved up. Being hit makes you long, so the quote moves down.
byKey.quarter: You used a skew of 0.25. This rule uses 0.5 a unit.

explain.text: Long 2 with $\gamma = 0.5$ moves the centre down 1, to 9.5. The quote is 8.5 at 10.5. Your ask now sits at fair value, so you are keen to sell.

items.prose: The interviewer rolls a die and looks. They buy above your ask and sell below your bid. You quote 2 at 4.
items.question: What is your average loss a game? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add how far each face lands outside the quote, then divide by 6.

byKey.count: You counted trades, 3 of 6. Weight each by how far outside it lands.

explain.text: Face 1 is 1 below the bid; faces 5 and 6 are 1 and 2 above the ask. That is 4 over six faces, 2/3. The quote is off centre, so the high side costs more.

items.prose: Three cards from one deck. The first two show a queen and a 5.
items.question: What is the fair value of the sum? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The last card averages $(364 - 17)/50$.

byKey.seven: You kept 7 for the last card. The deck has lost 17 points and 2 cards.
byKey.first: You used 51 cards. Two have left the deck, so 50 remain.

explain.text: The deck now holds $364 - 17 = 347$ points in 50 cards, 6.94 a card. The fair value is $17 + 6.94 = 23.94$. Two high-ish cards pulled the last card's mean below 7.

items.prose: Two dice, fair value 7. You quote 6 at 8. The interviewer buys 2 at 8. You skew to 6.5 at 8.5, and they sell you 1 at 6.5.
items.question: What is your P&L at fair, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Mark each trade at 7.

byKey.noskew: You marked the purchase at 6. You bought at your skewed bid, 6.5.
byKey.cash: That is your cash, 16 − 6.5. Mark against 7 instead.

explain.text: The sale of 2 at 8 earns 2, and the purchase at 6.5 earns 0.5. The total is £2.50, and you are short 1. The skew gave up 0.5 of edge to buy one back.

items.prose: You quote 9.5 at 11.5 on three dice. The interviewer has sold you 4 in a row.
items.question: Where should your quote go?

options.text: Up: they keep selling, so raise the bid and buy more.
options.why: You moved up. Long 4, buying more grows the position, so lower both prices.

options.text: Stay: the dice have not changed.
options.why: Your position has changed, even if the dice have not.
Moving only the bid slows buying but does not invite buyers. Move both down.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Long positions push the quote down.

explain.text: Being hit four times makes you long 4. A lower ask invites buyers, and a lower bid slows sellers. Both shrink the position.

items.prose: A share is worth 400p. A quarter of traders are informed about a move of 12p either way.
items.question: What ask breaks even, in pence?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The half-spread is $\alpha\delta$.

byKey.delta: You added the whole move. Only a quarter of traders know it.
byKey.full: You added the whole spread, $2\alpha\delta$. The ask is one half-spread above 400p.

explain.text: $s = 0.25 \times 12 = 3$p, so the ask is 403p and the bid 397p. Twice as many informed traders would double it. Twice the news would too.

items.prose: You sold 1 at 9 on two dice, fair value 7. The dice came up 11.
items.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: The sale had edge +2; the 11 was bad luck.
The sale was bad: it lost 2.
options.why: You judged the trade by one roll. Selling at 9 against 7 earns 2 on average.

options.text: The edge was 0, because wins and losses cancel.
options.why: They do not cancel: the sale wins on most rolls.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Judge the trade at its price.

explain.text: Selling at 9 a total worth 7 has edge +2. Only rolls of 10 to 12 lose, 1 time in 6. One bad roll does not change the edge.

items.prose: Two cards; the first shows a king. Compare one shared deck with a fresh deck for each card.
items.question: How much higher is the fair value with fresh decks? Give four decimal places.

byKey.zero: With one shared deck the king leaves it, so the second card averages less than 7.
byKey.seven: You took the shared deck’s mean as 6. It is $351/51$, so the gap is $7 - 351/51 = 2/17$.

explain.text: Shared: $13 + 351/51 = 19.8824$. Fresh: $13 + 7 = 20$. The gap, $7 - 351/51 = 6/51 = 2/17$, is the king missing from the shared deck.
